title: Paul's banjo, saxophone, WPA band, Eureka, clarinet and Thomas
summary: Paul tells of banjo, alto and soprano sax, the WPA band, joining the Eureka brass band, Bill Russell's clarinet, and working with Thomas.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, I played that for a while. Then later on, that, uh, fellas began falling out. Nice we had supposed to have had instructions. Fellas began having dates, you know. Couldn't come out to rehearsal, uh, instructions. So, therefore, that, uh, caused the band to disband, see. And, uh, from that, well, the fellas went astray. And, uh, I wonder if you can hear me. Yeah. Mm-hmm. So, therefore, that's, uh, that's where I started music, and from the church, on the violin. What instrument did you take? And you must have had another instrument after the violin. Yeah, after the violin, I played that for a little while. Yeah, I take an instruction on, uh, Professor Taylor, and later on the Professor Correa. Yeah, but you changed from violin. And, uh, from the violin, I changed to banjo. Mm-hmm. Which my wife, she made the present of a banjo, and... Which I take great interest in, and I bought myself a mortal method, and that is, taught myself how to play the banjo. Mm-hmm. And you can still play it, huh? Uh, yes, I still know a little of it. I'm not accustomed, I'm not practical to it like I used to be. But, although, I still understand it. What year you took up the banjo about? Around 25. Mm-hmm. Yeah, 25. And I played a... You were grown? Oh, quite naturally. I was 17 when I... And 21, so therefore, 25, uh, quite... Four years different. But anyway, that, uh... I played the banjo about four... About nine years. About nine to ten years. Then, I gave that up. And later, a friend was interested in me learning some other instrument. So, it was an alto saxophone. Mm-hmm. And I tried that for a while. Gave me some, you know, ideas of it. I like myself on it. On the alto sax. Then, later on, we, uh... I went on through playing with different fellows with the alto. Played with old man Jackson, the bass player. You remember him? Mm-hmm. We had a band, and... Is that Eddie Jackson? Eddie Jackson, yes. String bass at that band, or... Oh, he was playing the sousaphone. Mm-hmm. Yeah. And we played different places. As I played in the alto. And, uh, also Luce, I think Luce played with us too, if I'm not mistaken. Which Luce is that? That's, uh, Albert Jackson. Oh, Luce. Yeah. Oh, Luce, yeah. Mm-hmm. So, therefore, that, uh... I played with so many different fellows, and doing the WPA band. Of course, I played in that band too. Mm-hmm. From about 1934 to about 19... Say within all, the 41. Which saxophone did you play with them? Well, I played both. I played, uh... I played soprano, yeah. I played soprano sax. In fact, when I first got on there, I didn't have any instrument at all. Mm-hmm. I gave up all the playing during that time. That's during around about 1934. Mm-hmm. During that time, well, I had some misfortune during my labor. Oh, yeah. I was working for the bank. I worked for the bank for about, uh, 11 years. 1933, the bank closed down. Mm-hmm. And, 34 was a tough year for me. See, and I didn't have no instrument or nothing. And, most likely, that I, uh, picked up on... That is, they told me about this WPA band. And, which I got... I... That is, I registered in this WPA. And, so the fellow told me I had to have an instrument. So, I borrowed an instrument from a friend, which was an album. I mean, the soprano sax. That's all he had to line me. So, I went on in there as soprano sax player. I played that. So, it was one of those curved sopranos. So, later on, when I made a payday, I bought my own soprano. So, therefore, I played the soprano, straight soprano. Throughout the WPA up until about 1930... 36, I think it was. 1936. Then, later on, I got to be a tenor. Mm-hmm. See, and I played tenor in the WPA band. When did you get with the Eureka? Well, around 1944, I think. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I was 44. I joined... I was playing with T-Boy. T-Boy was the leader of the Eureka brass band. 38. Rami T-Boy. And, he asked me to play with him. I was playing at a nightclub with him. And, he asked me to play with him. I had never played with a brass band. I mean a film band, you know. And, he asked me to play with him. So, I started playing with him. And, from then on, up to now, I'm still playing with him. And, and... Had you played any parades with the brass bands before? No, I had never played any parades or fumes with any other bands. Neither fumes or parades. No. Oh, that's amazing that you can do that. Uh-huh. What about, uh... When did you take up the clarin? I was always curious about that. Well... Mr. Russell. Bill Russell. He, uh... He, uh... He, he was interested in my... I don't know. He considered that, uh, technical fingering on the teller. Seemed like he felt as though that I could be much greater on the, on a clarinet. Uh, clarinet. So, he, him and another fellow came to a place where I was playing across the river at the fireman hall and he asked me. Uh, the fellow came up and asked me, say, look, if I give you a clarinet, I said, he'd say, would you try to learn it? And I'd say, well, I, I don't know. I'd say, it's pretty late in years to try to learn a clarinet. I'd say, an instrument like that, you'd have to raise up with it. And I'd come up with it in order to master it, uh, get enough out of it that it would entertain the people. So, therefore, that... Yeah. Okay. So, therefore, that, uh... So, later on, uh, I say it's too old now. I don't think I'd be interested in it. So, I just gave, you know, just like, I don't know, that's that. So, later on, him and Raph came to my house and brought the clarinet. Raph Collins, yeah. And, uh, they brought it to my house and, uh, he said, well, we brought you one. He said, it's up to you now. He said, it's up to you. He's up to you. Try to learn it. Yeah, element system. Yeah, element system, yeah. So, I said, well, I'll try to do the best that I can. So, what happened, I did. I tried. So, that'd been about three, a little better than three years ago. Off and on. You see, I played a little bit, play with a little bit. I tried. Never did take no instructions on it. Whatsoever. Just called to the line and said, I... You know, got some books or something. I like that, Belgium, St. Mary. Yes, uh-huh. Just picked it up. That's all. Anything else. What about, uh, how long you been with Thomas? Oh, since about around the same time. Around about, like, 44, 45, something like that. Mm-hmm. Yes, because I was working... Not steady, though, huh? Study, yeah. It was pretty steady then. Because I was working during the day at the Naval Supply, right on the river on Napoleon Avenue. I was working there. I was working about 12 hours a day there, and then I'd leave, bring my everything that I had right there, and I'd leave my instrument over across the river. I'd leave from there and go to work across the river right there at the Napoleon Ferry. And we used to work from 10 to 12 hours a day, and I'd be still working with Thomas about three nights a week. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I'd work with him a long time. A very long time. You can read, huh? All the guys... Well, consider it, I did read. I liked to read, yeah, but as he has been past, you know, lots of music I'd forgotten. Yeah. It comes back to you, I noticed. Yeah, it comes back to me, but so little that I had to use it, you know, that just causes you to forget. Well, I noticed you got the sheet music on Jebouzaam. Oh, yeah, yeah. Well, I just... Okay. That's it, I'm afraid. Time's running out. We all right, huh? Yeah. We all right. We all right.
